query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the multiphase eutectic HEA, the coexistence of electrochemically dissimilar phases (for example, a softer FCC matrix and harder second-phase particles such as σ) promotes localized galvanic cells. Under elevated temperature wear conditions, repeated rupture of the protective oxide layer on the worn surface exposes fresh areas that are more susceptible to electrochemical attack. This wear–corrosion synergy, fueled by the galvanic coupling at phase boundaries, accelerates overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase microstructure (e.g., an FCC matrix with interspersed σ-phase or other hard second phases)
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to simultaneous mechanical (sliding or abrasive) wear and corrosive attack in a chloride-containing solution at elevated temperature
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., 600°C or similar regime where oxidation is prominent), a corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution), and applied mechanical wear (e.g., pin-on-disc sliding wear) to induce cyclic rupture of oxide films
generation.structural_mediator: The spatial juxtaposition and intimate contact of dissimilar phases that have differing electrochemical potentials, fostering galvanic interactions particularly at phase boundaries
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, a protective oxide film forms on the alloy surface. Mechanical wear intermittently disrupts this film, exposing fresh metal. Because the constituent phases have different corrosion potentials, galvanic cells form at their interfaces, intensifying localized corrosion. This localized attack not only weakens the oxide’s integrity but also increases the abrasive removal of material, thereby accelerating the overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a homogeneous (single-phase) HEA baseline, the multiphase eutectic alloy will show a higher total degradation rate. Both the wear rate (due to more frequent oxide film rupture and abrasive particle generation) and the corrosion rate (due to strong galvanic interactions at phase interfaces) are predicted to be elevated.
generation.baseline: A matched high-entropy alloy with a single-phase (homogeneous) microstructure subjected to the same elevated temperature, corrosive (e.g., chloride-containing solution), and applied mechanical wear conditions
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions where elevated temperatures promote stable yet rupture-prone oxide films and where simultaneous mechanical wear in a corrosive medium is active. It may not hold for lower temperatures or in the absence of significant mechanical wear.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details (e.g., exact increases in wear volume or corrosion current density) depend on specific compositions and operating conditions; the relative contribution of galvanic effects versus mechanical rupture requires further precise measurement.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of coatings: one with the eutectic, multiphase microstructure and one with a comparable single-phase HEA. Expose both sets to identical conditions—elevated temperature, a chloride-containing corrosive medium, and controlled sliding wear (using a pin-on-disc setup). Monitor and compare oxide layer integrity, corrosion rates (via electrochemical techniques), and wear volumes.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion current density and impedance
Wear rate (mm³/N·m) via weight loss or profilometry
Surface potential mapping to detect galvanic cells
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multiphase eutectic alloy does not exhibit statistically significant higher corrosion rates and wear losses—especially evidence of galvanic interaction at phase boundaries—compared to the single-phase baseline under identical testing conditions, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis (galvanic coupling combined with cyclic oxide rupture driving accelerated degradation) is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

This study systematically investigates the microstructure evolution, tribological properties, and corrosion mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings fabricated via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding under variable laser power conditions. The key findings and implications are summarized as follows: The CoCrFeNiMo coatings exhibited a dual-phase structure comprising FCC and σ phases. At 2250 W, optimized energy density promoted homogeneous dispersion of Fe-Cr-rich σa and Fe-Mo-rich σb phases within the FCC matrix, forming a refined eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure. The hardness of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings increased with laser power, peaking at 738.3 HV0.2 at 2250 W. This improvement was attributed to solution strengthening and second-phase intensification. However, at 2000 W, the hardness decreased due to grain coarsening caused by the extended molten pool duration. At a laser power of 2250 W, the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (COF = 0.084) and excellent wear resistance.
